title: The self's first word
hookLine: the first thing the self ever said was 'I am'
carry: the I before every name is Brahman
tomorrow: the first feeling in the story isn't joy. what is it?

cards: Somebody knocks. Who is it? And almost nobody answers with a name.
It's me. The name comes second, if it comes at all. The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad noticed that habit at the door, and its explanation starts before anything existed.
The self is alone, in the shape of a person. It looks around and sees nothing but itself. And then, for the first time ever, it speaks.

teach.b: The first thing it says, the text tells us, is: I am. Aham asmi. And so, the story says, it came to be called I.
Then the Upanishad steps out of the beginning and into an ordinary doorway.
That's why, even now, when someone is called, they first answer, it's I, and only after that give whatever other name they have. Look at the order. I comes first.

teach.h: EVERY OTHER NAME IS ADDED ON.
teach.b: Every other name comes after: a family name, a nickname, a major, someone's daughter, someone's dad. They're real, and they matter. In this story they're added on.
The plain I underneath them is what Hindus call the atman, the self. Now the saying this week is named for.
A few verses later, the same chapter says that in the beginning this was Brahman, and it knew itself only: aham brahmasmi. I am Brahman.

teach.h: AHAM: THE STORY'S WORD, THE SAYING'S WORD.
teach.b: Aham, the very first word of the story, is the first word of the saying. So the great saying doesn't start up in the sky and work its way down to a person.
It starts where the self in the story started, and where every answer at a door starts. With I.
What the saying adds is the boldest claim in the Upanishads: that this plain I, the atman, is Brahman, the reality behind everything.

how: In the Advaita tradition, aham brahmasmi is studied in its Brihadaranyaka setting with a teacher and reflected on in meditation; other Vedanta schools read the 'I' in their own ways.

o: I am Brahman: the self is the one reality
I serve Brahman: a vow a student makes
I seek Brahman: a seeker's opening prayer

games.q: the first word. tap the pairs.
p: the I first, the name after

s: aham brahmasmi means 'my personality is God'
in the story the I comes before every other name; the saying points at that plain I, not the personality.
the Brihadaranyaka explains why people answer 'it's me' before their name
the self's first word was I am; so even now, the I comes first and the other name after.
in this story, the self speaks only after it makes a world
it speaks while it's alone, seeing nothing but itself.

games.q: a friend introduces herself only by her school and her job, then freezes when someone asks, 'but who are you?' by the Brihadaranyaka's story, what's going on?
o: those names came second; the plain I came first, and it's still there.
she has no self at all apart from her school and job.
she just needs a more impressive job title to say.
games.why: in the story, I am is the first word, and every other name is added after it. the second names are real; they just aren't the first one.

practice: Say your own name once, quietly, out loud. Then say just: I am. Notice the difference: the name has a history, a family, a spelling; the I am is plainer, and in the story it came first.
Rest with the plain one, saying it once more whenever the mind wanders off.

wordCard.voice: Aham brahmasmi: I am Brahman, the great saying of the Brihadaranyaka. Today's piece of it is the first word, aham: I.

orig.note: Sanskrit aham, I: the self's first word in the Brihadaranyaka's story, and the first word of aham brahmasmi.

carryVoice: Here's one to keep: the I before every name is Brahman. That's aham brahmasmi. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 1.4.1 (in the beginning this was the self alone, in the shape of a person; looking around it saw nothing but itself; it first said 'I am', and so became I by name; so even now one who is called first says 'it is I', then gives whatever other name he has)
Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 1.4.10 (in the beginning this was Brahman; it knew itself only: I am Brahman)
